pages.title: About
pages.content:
About

the clinic since 2011

Hitomi Vision is an independent optometry clinic on the second floor of 14 Linden Row, Northgate. We opened in 2011 and we still see office workers and school-age children in three exam rooms and a small frame room.

The clinic in 2011

since 2011

Hitomi Vision opened in 2011 on the second floor of 14 Linden Row, Northgate. A lift comes up from the street door. There were three exam rooms and a small frame room then, and those are still the rooms we work in. The waiting area was a pale sofa, a side table, and a plant. People who have been coming for years recognise that corner before they recognise any piece of equipment.

The clinic was opened for two groups we still book every week: adults who spend the day at a screen, and children of school age. A visit is an appointment with a named clinician. The comprehensive exam is sixty minutes. When the question is narrower, the book has a shorter visit, and every fee is published in US dollars before you arrive.

The front window on Linden Row shows plants and a pale frame display. We have kept the address and stayed independent. Current instruments matter, and so does this: the person who measured you is in the building when the plan is explained. You leave with the findings said aloud, and with the fee already on the list.

Office workers and school desks

adults and children

Office workers usually arrive with a clock time. Tired eyes by four o'clock, blur that grows after a long stretch at a monitor, a dry burning feeling, and a neck that has been helping the eyes cope. Those are the symptoms we take in the first ten minutes of a history. Screen distance, a near add, and the way the two eyes hold a target are things we can measure. Dr. Jonah Whitfield leads the screen and workplace work. Dr. Elena Marsh leads adult binocular vision.

School-age children arrive with a different list, and with a parent. A book held close, lines skipped, reading avoided, eyes rubbed, the board soft from the back of the room. Ages five to fifteen are seen by Dr. Tomas Reyes. The test uses games and picture targets when a letter chart is not fair. Myopia, when we find it, is reviewed every six months.

We keep both groups in one clinic because the sequence is the same. History, refraction, binocular vision, eye health, then a plan. The rooms are shared. The questions are not blurred together.

2011

today

2011 and today

then and now

Two photographs sit with this account of the building. One is the waiting room: pale sofa, side table, plant, empty of people, the light of the row coming in. Its caption is 2011. The other is the front window as you meet it from the street now: plants, a pale frame display, no large sign. Its caption is today.

We keep the pair because the clinic is easier to read when the address has stayed put. Second floor, lift from the street door, three exam rooms, one frame room. If you are coming for the first time, the window is what you look for on Linden Row. At the top of the lift, Hana Lindgren meets you at the desk. The exam rooms are just beyond that waiting room.

The photographs are of the rooms, not of a renovation story. We still answer the phone on +1 555 0142 208 and email at hello@hitomivision.example.

Dr. Elena Marsh

founder and director

At the slit lamp,
then the explanation.

Dr. Elena Marsh, OD, is founder and director. Her clinical work is with adults, and with binocular vision: how the two eyes aim, focus, and stay comfortable at the distance the work actually uses. She is often at the slit lamp, and she still expects the last part of a comprehensive exam to be a conversation. Fifteen minutes of the sixty are kept for the explanation and the plan.

She does not see every person who books. Dr. Tomas Reyes sees children's vision and myopia follow-up. Dr. Priya Nair sees dry eye and contact lenses. Dr. Jonah Whitfield sees screen and workplace vision. Ines Kowalczyk fits frames and lenses. Samuel Achebe is the clinical technician for imaging. Hana Lindgren runs the front desk and the book.

Ask for Dr. Marsh by name when the question is an adult binocular one. If another clinician is the better match, the desk will say so when you book. The director's photograph on this page is her at the slit lamp.

How we practise

how we work

We measure, and then we advise. A headache at four, a skipped line, a lens that stings by evening: each can have more than one cause. The exam is how we separate them. An individual account on this site is one person's record. Results differ. We can measure your eyes. We cannot promise you someone else's afternoon.

We keep time for the explanation. In the comprehensive exam the last fifteen minutes are the plan: what was found, what we suggest, what it costs, and what a follow-up is for. A follow-up check within six months is twenty minutes and $40. You should be able to say, in your own words, which part was the refraction and which part was distance, habit, or the tear film.

We stay small enough to know the book. Three exam rooms and a frame room means the clinician, the technician, the optician, and the desk share one corridor. The published hours are the real hours. Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00, Saturday 9:00–16:00, Sunday and public holidays closed.

pages.title: Eye Exams
pages.content:
Eye Exams

one hour, five stages

A comprehensive eye exam at Hitomi Vision is sixty minutes and $120. It is one sitting in one room: five stages, and time at the end to go through the plan.

The sixty-minute exam

five stages, one hour

History and symptoms, ten minutes. We ask what fails and when: blur after screens, a headache by four o'clock, a burn that arrives late in the day, a child who skips lines. We note the glasses or contact lenses you already wear, and the work or the classroom those eyes have to serve.

Refraction, fifteen minutes. You look through the phoropter while we find the lens that clears the chart. This stage answers how much lens the eye wants at distance and at near. For a child who is not a confident reader, picture targets and games carry the same question.

Binocular vision and working distance, ten minutes. We look at how the two eyes work as a pair, and we measure the distance you actually use. A monitor and a road sign are different tasks.

Eye health and tear film imaging, ten minutes. The slit lamp, and a retinal image when the plan needs one, show the surface, the lids, and the structures we are there to see. A short tear break-up time is written down.

Explanation and plan, fifteen minutes. We say what we found, what we suggest, and what it will cost. The hour is $120.

What we measure

lens and tissue

Refraction:
the lens that clears
the chart.

Refraction is the lens. It tells us what clears the chart in the chair. It does not, by itself, tell us whether you can hold that focus at a desk, or whether a child's two eyes point at the same place on the board. Binocular testing sits beside the refraction for that reason, and it is part of the same hour, not an extra product.

The slit lamp:
the surface, the lids,
the tear film.

Eye health is the tissue. At the slit lamp we look at the cornea, the tear film, and the lids. When imaging belongs in the visit, Samuel Achebe, the clinical technician, runs the retinal camera. The picture is a record for the optometrist to read with you in the explanation. It is described in ordinary words.

The two photographs on this page are those stages: refraction at the phoropter, and the slit lamp with the chin on the rest. They are the middle of the hour. The history comes before them, and the plan comes after. Nothing in the hour is a step you have to interpret alone.

What to bring

before you come

Bring the glasses you wear now, and any contact lenses, with their case and the name of the solution or the lens. If you use drops, bring the names. An old prescription is useful as history, and we will measure again rather than copy it. Children do not need to prepare a reading test at home. A note from school about the board or about skipped lines is worth handing to Dr. Tomas Reyes if you have one.

Come as you are. The rooms are bright, and the visit is one appointment in one exam room. If the question is only the desk, only dryness, or only a child between five and fifteen, say so when you book. Those visits have their own length and their own fee, and they are the better use of the chair when the comprehensive hour is more than you need.

If you already know you want frames, you can see Ines Kowalczyk after the explanation, or on another day. Lenses are quoted once the prescription and the working distance are known.

The fee

one fee, in us dollars

The comprehensive eye exam is sixty minutes and $120. The fee covers the five stages, including the explanation. It does not include frames or lenses. Frames start at $160. Lenses are quoted after the exam. The same prices are published in every language, in US dollars.

A narrower question has a narrower visit. The screen-work eye assessment is forty-five minutes and $85. The dry eye evaluation is forty minutes and $90. The children's vision exam, ages five to fifteen, is fifty minutes and $95. A contact lens fitting, including two follow-ups, is $110. A follow-up check within six months of an exam here is twenty minutes and $40.

Book on +1 555 0142 208 or at hello@hitomivision.example. Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00, Saturday 9:00–16:00. Sunday and public holidays the clinic is closed. Ask for Dr. Elena Marsh if you want the director for an adult binocular case.

pages.title: Children's Vision
pages.content:
Children's Vision

ages five to fifteen

Children's vision exams are for ages five to fifteen. The visit is fifty minutes and $95, with Dr. Tomas Reyes, and it can be booked in the after-school slots.

Signs at school

signs at school

A book held close
is something we can
measure.

Teachers and parents tend to notice the same cluster, and none of it is a diagnosis from the doorway. The book migrates toward the face. Lines are skipped, or a finger stays under the words. Reading is avoided, especially aloud, and a task that was fine in a short burst becomes a fight at homework time. From the back of the room the board is soft, so the child copies a neighbour or waits for a sheet. Eyes are rubbed, particularly late in the school day.

Bring that description with you. It belongs in the history. A mild myopia and a focusing difficulty can look alike across a classroom, which is why we would rather measure than guess from the story alone. Ages five to fifteen are the range of this visit. A parent is in the room.

The photograph of reading on this page is a girl of about nine with the book held close. That posture is a reason to book. It is not yet a prescription. Dr. Tomas Reyes sorts out which cause is actually there.

How we test ages five to fifteen

games, not a reading test

The children's vision exam is fifty minutes. It does not depend on a child being able to read rows of letters. Where reading is shaky, or not yet there, Dr. Tomas Reyes uses games and picture targets. The clinical questions are still covered: how the eyes focus, how the two eyes work together, and whether the eyes are healthy. The history comes from the parent. When did the book get close? What did the teacher say about the board? Are there headaches?

We explain the result to the adult in the room, and to the child in language that matches their age. First glasses, when they are needed, are fitted in the frame room by Ines Kowalczyk, with the parent there. A child is given time at the frame wall. The frame is part of wearing the prescription, and it can happen on the same afternoon when the frame room is free. When it is not, Hana Lindgren books a fitting of its own.

The fee for this exam is $95. It is the same fee in every after-school slot.

Myopia follow-up every six months

every six months

When we find myopia, the first pair is the start of the record. Follow-up is every six months. A follow-up check within six months of an exam at the clinic is twenty minutes and $40. We use that visit so a change is written against the last numbers, while the child is still wearing the prescription, rather than left until a later school screening.

Each return uses the same questions. The same distances. The same symptoms. A small shift is then visible. A front-row seat is sometimes part of the note to school. It is a seating suggestion so the board is usable while the glasses do their work. We say that plainly to parents, and we write it as a suggestion.

L., whose account is below, is on this six-month rhythm. Your child enters it only if myopia is what we measured. If the finding is different, the plan is different, and we will say what the next visit is for before you leave.

week 0, the frame wall

week 6, the front row

L., age nine

one account

L. is nine and in primary school. The history was board blur and skipped lines. On examination there was mild myopia of −1.25 in both eyes. The plan was a first pair of glasses, a front-row seat, and follow-up every six months.

The photographs with this account are the frame wall and the classroom. One shows a boy trying frames with a parent at the pale wood wall. The other shows a boy of that age reading the board in new glasses. Captions sit with the pair as a record of the kind of visit: first frames, then the board. L.'s measurement is −1.25 in both eyes. That figure is hers. It is not a prediction for the next child who skips a line.

This is an individual account. Results differ. We measured L., we fitted a first pair, and we booked the six-month check. A parent who recognises the signs can book the children's exam and let the refraction speak for itself. The signs are a reason to come. The numbers are what we find in the room.

Fee and after-school slots

fee and slots

The children's vision exam for ages five to fifteen is fifty minutes and $95. After-school slots are Monday to Friday, 15:30–18:30, and Saturday, 9:00–12:00. The clinic is otherwise open Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00 and Saturday 9:00–16:00, and it is closed on Sunday and public holidays. The children's slots sit inside those hours. They are held for this exam, with Dr. Tomas Reyes.

Say your child's age when you book, so Hana Lindgren can offer one of those slots rather than an adult visit in the same hour. Phone +1 555 0142 208 or email hello@hitomivision.example. Bring any glasses already worn. A school note about the board is useful if you have it. The book they actually read is useful too, because the distance we care about is the one they use, not a distance performed for a stranger.

Frames, if a first pair is needed, start at $160. Lenses are quoted after the exam.

pages.title: Screen and Workplace Eyes
pages.content:
Screen and Workplace Eyes

the working distance

The screen-work eye assessment is forty-five minutes and $85. It is for eyes that tire at the desk, and it measures distance, lens, and how the two eyes hold a near task.

The working distance

a measurable distance

Four o’clock is a
time we can write
down.

We measure the distance from your eyes to the screen you actually use. In the account of M., an accountant of 46, the monitor sat at 55 cm. After the assessment it was moved to 65 cm. Those two figures are hers. Yours will be whatever we measure on the day. A screen held close asks for more focusing effort for more of the day, and the number goes down in the record before anyone talks about lenses.

We also ask when the symptoms arrive. Tired eyes by four o'clock, a headache that settles in mid-afternoon, blur that clears on the way home: the timing is part of the history. Dr. Jonah Whitfield leads this work. The screen-work eye assessment is forty-five minutes and $85.

Bring the glasses you use at the desk, even if you think of them as "old". If you can, know the distance before you come. If you cannot, we will measure a comparable distance here and ask you to confirm it against your own monitor. The plan uses your number.

Monitor height and the 20-20-20 habit

monitor height and breaks

Monitor height is the other half of the desk. A screen set high leaves the lids open and the surface dries. A screen set low recruits the neck. We look at the height you use and suggest a change you can make with the stand you already have. We are here for the eyes. Neck tension is often part of the story you tell, and we listen to it as a clue to the desk, then we send musculoskeletal care to the people who provide it.

The 20-20-20 habit is a break we will talk through when it belongs in the plan. Every twenty minutes, look at something about twenty feet away, for about twenty seconds. It is a pause for focus and for blinking. It does not replace a lens the refraction has shown you need. Many people who come for this assessment have no pause in the afternoon at all. We would rather add a pause to a measured plan than offer the pause as the whole plan.

Dr. Whitfield will say whether the habit earns a place. If your symptom is blur that never clears, the phoropter comes first.

Occupational lenses

lenses for the desk

Occupational lenses are built for a range of near distances. In M.'s account the near add was +0.75, and the lenses were specified for 50–70 cm: the band between a document and a monitor. They were for that band. They were a poor choice for driving, and we said so. Her screen then moved from 55 cm to 65 cm, inside the range the lenses were made for.

That is one prescription. It is not a package handed to everyone with a laptop. Distance glasses, a separate pair for the desk, or occupational lenses are three different answers. The assessment tells us which one matches the way you work. The fee does not include the lenses. Frames start at $160, and lenses are quoted after the exam, once the prescription and the working distance are both known.

Ines Kowalczyk fits the frame and checks that the lens type on the order matches the range we wrote down. You can take the prescription away and decide later. The quote will still be in US dollars, the same in every language.

week 0, 4 pm, second coffee

week 6, same desk, new lenses

M., age 46, accountant

one account

M. is 46 and works as an accountant. She came because of headaches at four in the afternoon. Her screen sat at 55 cm. We measured a near add of +0.75 and prescribed occupational lenses for 50–70 cm. She moved the screen to 65 cm. At the six-week check she reported afternoons without headaches.

The photographs are the desk before and after. One caption reads: week 0 — 4 pm, second coffee. She is leaning toward the monitor, a slight squint, the day still in front of her. The other reads: week 6 — same desk, new lenses. Thin metal glasses, sitting upright, the same kind of work.

This is an individual account. Results differ. We cannot promise the same result. We can measure your distance, your add, and your symptoms, and we can tell you what we would change. A headache can have causes this clinic does not treat. What we report is what we measured, what we changed, and what M. said at six weeks.

The assessment fee

the assessment fee

The screen-work eye assessment is forty-five minutes and $85. It covers the history of the desk, refraction as it relates to that work, binocular vision at your working distance, and a plan. It is a focused visit. When the findings need the longer look at eye health, we say so and book the comprehensive exam, which is sixty minutes and $120.

A follow-up check within six months is twenty minutes and $40. M.'s review at six weeks was that kind of return to the record. Your review is booked for the question we actually left open.

Hours are Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00 and Saturday 9:00–16:00. Sunday and public holidays are closed. Phone +1 555 0142 208 or email hello@hitomivision.example and ask for a screen-work assessment with Dr. Jonah Whitfield. If dryness is the larger complaint, the dry eye evaluation may be the better first hour. The desk will help you choose.

pages.title: Dry Eye and Contact Lenses
pages.content:
Dry Eye and Contact Lenses

the tear film

Dry eye evaluations are forty minutes and $90. A contact lens fitting, including two follow-ups, is $110. Dr. Priya Nair leads both, from the tear film to the lens you take home.

Tear film

surface and lids

The tear film is the surface you look through. When it breaks up quickly, the world can be sharp for a moment and then smear, especially in a warm office or at a bright screen. We time that break-up. We do not ask you to rank the burn and then guess. The dry eye evaluation is forty minutes and $90, with Dr. Priya Nair.

The visit includes a history of when the discomfort arrives, a look at the lids and the surface at the slit lamp, and tear film imaging when it will change the plan. Burning by evening, contact lenses that are fine at breakfast and poor at dinner, and a reflex to close the eyes at the laptop are typical reasons to book this visit. If you also need a full refraction, we schedule the comprehensive exam, sixty minutes and $120, rather than pretend it fits inside forty minutes.

The photograph of contact-lens teaching on this page is the practical part of a fitting: a lens, a patient, and enough time to learn the hands. The evaluation itself may stop at the surface, with no lens at all.

Lid care

lid care

Lid care is a routine we teach in the room. We show you how to warm the lids, how long the warmth stays, and how to clean along the lash line. A warm compress in the treatment chair is sometimes the first time the feeling is specific: a sore surface, or a lid that is simply not flowing as it should. You leave able to repeat the routine on a weekday morning.

We teach what we have looked at. If the surface is inflamed in a way that belongs with your physician, we say so and we write it down. The compress is part of lid care for the finding we made. It is not a substitute for a refraction, and it is not a substitute for medical care that sits outside this clinic.

D., the engineer in the account below, started here. His compress photograph is the treatment chair in daylight, mask on, the visit still quiet. The routine only mattered because the tear film finding was already on the record.

Daily lenses and two follow-ups

fitting and follow-ups

Insertion and removal,
taught in the room.

Some eyes do better in a lens that is thrown away at the end of the day. Daily lenses are the option we use when a longer-wear lens is drying out by evening, or when solution and the case have become part of the irritation. Dr. Priya Nair does the fitting. Samuel Achebe does not fit lenses; he runs imaging when imaging is required.

The contact lens fitting is $110 and includes two follow-ups. The first visit is the fit: lens type, the way it moves, the vision through it, and teaching you to put it in and take it out. The two follow-ups exist so we see the eye after real days of wear. Those two visits are inside the $110. A different return, the general follow-up check within six months, is twenty minutes and $40, and it is a separate fee when it is not one of the included two.

If you already wear lenses, bring them, the boxes, and the solution you use. We need the names. If you would rather wear glasses for part of the day, frames start at $160 and are quoted with lenses after the prescription is known.

week 0, the compress chair

week 8, evening, no burn

D., age 31, software engineer

one account

D. is 31 and works as a software engineer. His eyes burned, and his contact lenses were uncomfortable by evening. We measured a short tear break-up time. The plan was a lid care routine, a move to daily lenses, and 20-20-20 breaks through the workday. At eight weeks he was comfortable through the workday.

The photographs beside this account are the two ends of that plan. One is a man in his thirties with a warm compress in the bright treatment chair. The other is a man of that age at a desk in the evening, eyes comfortable, a glass of water, a laptop. The eight-week picture is the review, not a promise about the eighth week for anyone else.

This is an individual account. Results differ. Three things changed at once: the lids, the lens, and the breaks. We will not point at one of them and call it the reason. We will look at your tear film, your lenses, and your day, and we will write a plan that belongs to those findings.

Fees for this work

fees for this work

Two fees live on this page. The dry eye evaluation is forty minutes and $90. The contact lens fitting is $110 and includes two follow-ups, so those return visits are not billed again. A follow-up check within six months that is outside those included visits is twenty minutes and $40.

Frames, when glasses are the better part-day answer, start at $160. Lenses are quoted after we know the prescription. Prices are in US dollars and they are the same in every language.

Book on +1 555 0142 208 or at hello@hitomivision.example. Ask for Dr. Priya Nair, and say whether you want the dry eye evaluation, the contact lens fitting, or both scheduled in the right order. Hours are Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00 and Saturday 9:00–16:00. Sunday and public holidays are closed. Bring the lenses you actually wear, including the pair that fails after lunch.

pages.title: Frames and Lenses
pages.content:
Frames and Lenses

the frame room

The frame room is a small room next to the exam rooms. Frames start at $160, lenses are quoted after the exam, and Ines Kowalczyk does the fitting.

The frame room

the frame room

Trial lenses, chosen
by the distance you
work at.

The frame room is the small room beside the three exam rooms. It is not a separate shop you walk through to reach the chair. You come here after the explanation, or on a later visit if you want to think first. A tray of trial lenses and a trial frame is how we are still deciding a prescription. The wall of frames is how we choose what you will wear once that prescription is known.

The selection is sized to be fitted in one sitting: a range of bridges and eyesizes, metal and acetate, quiet shapes. Frames start at $160. If a frame costs more than that starting figure, Ines Kowalczyk tells you the price before anything is glazed. You see the frame, the amount in US dollars, and the way it sits on the face.

The photographs on this page are the tray of trial lenses and the frame wall. One of them includes a boy trying frames with a parent. Children are given that time. Adults are given the same honesty about price and fit.

Fitting with Ines Kowalczyk

fitting

Ines Kowalczyk

Frames are tried
with a parent beside
the child.

Ines Kowalczyk is the optician. She fits frames and lenses. She does not refract. Bring the prescription we have just written, or an outside prescription if you are here only for glasses, and she will check that the lens type matches the way you work. A screen distance that was measured in the exam is written on the order, so an occupational lens is made for that range and not for a generic near.

A child at the frame wall has a parent in the room. Ines leaves time for the child to look up, look down, and forget they are being watched. An adult who needs a thin metal frame, or a deeper acetate, is told what the fit is doing at the bridge and the side.

Adjustments after you have worn the glasses are part of her work. If something presses or slides, come back to the frame room. You do not have to save that comment for the six-month check. If the prescription itself seems wrong, she will send you back to the optometrist rather than keep bending the frame to compensate.

Lens types

lens types

We describe lenses in words. Single-vision lenses do one distance. When the day is mostly far vision, they may be the whole order. Occupational lenses cover a set near range. In the account of M. that range was 50–70 cm, with a near add of +0.75, for documents and a monitor. Occupational lenses are a poor choice for driving, and we say so before they are made. A separate pair for distance and a separate pair for the desk is sometimes the clearer answer, and we price it that way when it is the honest recommendation.

Lenses are quoted after the exam because the quote depends on the prescription and on the working distance. There is no lens price on the fee list, and we will not invent one to make the page look complete. Frames from $160 are the figure we can publish. The lens quote is a conversation with the numbers we measured.

The same quoting rule, and the same frame starting price, apply in every language. The currency is US dollars.

From the order to collection

order to collection

When you agree a frame and a lens type, the order is written with your name, the measurements Ines takes on the frame, and the date you can collect. We tell you that collection day when we order. We do not print a single turnaround and pretend every lens is the same job. Collection is from this room.

If the glasses are for a child, we check the fit again at collection and show the parent how the sides should sit. If they are occupational lenses, we ask you to look at a screen-like distance in the room before you leave, so the first test of the range is not on Monday morning at your own desk. The exam fee and the glasses are separate charges. You will have heard both figures before you agree.

Book a frame visit on +1 555 0142 208 or at hello@hitomivision.example. Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00, Saturday 9:00–16:00. Sunday and public holidays closed. If you still need the exam, book that first. Frames without a current prescription are a guess, and we would rather measure.

pages.title: Fees
pages.content:
Fees

in us dollars

All clinical fees are in US dollars, and they are the same in every language. Six visits are listed here. Frames start at $160, and lenses are quoted after the exam.

Comprehensive eye exam

60 min

$120

Children’s vision exam (ages 5–15)

50 min

$95

Screen-work eye assessment

45 min

$85

Dry eye evaluation

40 min

$90

Contact lens fitting (incl. 2 follow-ups)

$110

Follow-up check within 6 months

20 min

$40

Frames from $160, lenses quoted after the exam. Same prices in every language.

Six fees, and what each includes

what each includes

Comprehensive eye exam, 60 min, $120. History and symptoms, refraction, binocular vision and working distance, eye health and tear film imaging, and the explanation and plan.

Children's vision exam, ages 5–15, 50 min, $95. Games and picture targets when reading a chart is not fair, a parent in the room, and a plan that includes six-month myopia follow-up when myopia is found.

Screen-work eye assessment, 45 min, $85. Working distance, monitor height, binocular vision at that distance, and a decision about occupational lenses, a desk pair, or distance glasses.

Dry eye evaluation, 40 min, $90. History, slit lamp, tear film, lids, and a routine you can repeat at home when lid care is the finding.

Contact lens fitting, including two follow-ups, $110. The fit, insertion and removal, and two return visits after real wear. No separate duration is published for the fitting visit; the two follow-ups are part of the fee.

Follow-up check within 6 months, 20 min, $40. A return after an exam here, when those minutes are not already included in a contact lens fitting.

Frames, lenses, and receipts

frames, lenses, receipts

Frames start at $160. Lenses are quoted after the exam, once the prescription and the working distance are known. Those two sentences are the whole of the glasses price list we publish. Same prices in every language. The currency on every page is US dollars. We do not convert the six fees.

Ask for a receipt. It shows the service, the date, the clinician, and the amount in US dollars. You may pass that receipt to an insurer if your own policy accepts care outside its panel. What the policy reimburses is between you and the insurer. The amount on the receipt is the amount paid at the clinic: $120, $95, $85, $90, $110, or $40, plus any frame and any lens quote you have agreed.

The price table is the full list of clinical fees. Nothing clinical is added at the desk. If a frame costs more than the $160 starting point, you hear that figure before it is ordered, from Ines Kowalczyk.

Questions

about fees

What does the $120 comprehensive exam include?

The $120 pays for sixty minutes and five stages. Ten minutes of history and symptoms. Fifteen minutes of refraction. Ten minutes of binocular vision and working distance. Ten minutes of eye health and tear film imaging. Fifteen minutes of explanation and plan. The hour is designed so the explanation is inside the fee, not a favour added at the door.

Imaging, when the plan needs a retinal photograph, is part of that eye-health stage. Samuel Achebe runs the camera. The optometrist reads it with you. Frames and lenses are outside the $120. Frames start at $160, and lenses are quoted afterwards.

A follow-up check within six months is a separate visit: twenty minutes, $40. Ask for Dr. Elena Marsh if you want the founder for an adult binocular case. The other optometrists lead the children's, dry-eye, and screen visits, which are the shorter fees on this page.

Why are lenses not listed as a fee?

A lens price depends on the prescription and on the distance you work at. Occupational lenses for a range such as 50–70 cm are a different order from single-vision distance lenses, and a second pair for the desk is different again. Publishing one lens price would invent a figure the exam has not earned. We quote lenses after the exam, in US dollars, and we use the same rule in every language.

Frames can start at a published figure because the frame room has a starting price. That figure is $160. Anything above it is said aloud by Ines Kowalczyk before you agree. The quote for the lenses is said in the same conversation.

You may take the prescription and think. The clinical fee you have already paid — $120, $95, $85, or whichever visit you booked — stands on its own. Glasses are a second decision. Many people make it on the day. Some come back.

When is the follow-up $40, and when is it already included?

A follow-up check within six months of an exam at this clinic is twenty minutes and $40. It is the return visit for a finding we want to see again: the six-week review in an adult case, the six-month myopia review for a child, or a question we deliberately left open at the end of the hour.

The contact lens fitting is the exception that is written on the list. That fee is $110 and includes two follow-ups. Those two visits are for judging the lens after real wear. You are not also charged $40 for them. A later check that is not one of those two, and that still falls within six months of an exam, is the $40 visit.

Children with myopia are reviewed every six months. When that review falls within six months of the last exam here, the published price of the review is $40 for twenty minutes. The original children's exam remains $95.

Can I book a shorter visit than sixty minutes?

Yes. Sixty minutes is the comprehensive eye exam, at $120. The other clinical visits are shorter, and each has its own fee.

Children's vision exam, ages five to fifteen: fifty minutes, $95, with Dr. Tomas Reyes. Screen-work eye assessment: forty-five minutes, $85, with Dr. Jonah Whitfield. Dry eye evaluation: forty minutes, $90, with Dr. Priya Nair. Contact lens fitting, including two follow-ups: $110, also with Dr. Nair. Follow-up check within six months: twenty minutes, $40.

Say which question you are bringing. Hana Lindgren will put the right length in the book. If the shorter visit shows that you need the comprehensive hour, we tell you and we schedule it. We would rather add the $120 visit honestly than stretch a forty-minute evaluation into work it does not contain.

Hours for all of these are Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00 and Saturday 9:00–16:00.

Do children's after-school slots use a different fee?

The children's vision exam is $95 for fifty minutes in the after-school slots and at any other time that exam is booked. The slots are Monday to Friday 15:30–18:30 and Saturday 9:00–12:00. They are a way of holding the book for ages five to fifteen. They are not a second price list.

Dr. Tomas Reyes sees those visits. A parent stays. Games and picture targets are used when a letter chart is not fair. If myopia is found, follow-up is every six months, and the follow-up check within six months is twenty minutes and $40.

The clinic's wider hours are Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00 and Saturday 9:00–16:00. Sunday and public holidays are closed. Phone +1 555 0142 208 or email hello@hitomivision.example and give your child's age so the slot offered is a children's slot. Frames, if a first pair is needed, still start at $160 and are quoted separately.

Are these prices the same in every language?

Yes. The site can be read in more than one language. The fees stay in US dollars, and they stay at the six figures on this page: $120, $95, $85, $90, $110, and $40. Frames still start at $160. Lenses are still quoted after the exam. We do not convert, and we do not publish a second table.

The address is the same in every language: 2nd floor, 14 Linden Row, Northgate. The phone is +1 555 0142 208. The email is hello@hitomivision.example. The hours are Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00 and Saturday 9:00–16:00, with Sunday and public holidays closed.

A receipt is in US dollars as well. It lists the service, the date, the clinician, and the amount you paid. Bring that receipt to an insurer if you wish. The clinic fee is the figure on this page, whichever language you used when you booked.

pages.title: Case Stories
pages.content:
Case Stories

individual accounts

Three accounts from the clinic, each about one person. They are individual accounts, and results differ. We cannot promise the same result. We can measure.

week 0, 4 pm, second coffee

week 6, same desk, new lenses

M., 46, accountant

case one

M. is 46 and works as an accountant. She booked because headaches arrived around four o'clock and stayed for the rest of the desk day. In the history she described a screen that had crept closer over months. We measured it at 55 cm. Refraction found a near add of +0.75. Distance vision and the monitor were not the same task, which is why a single distance pair would have been the wrong order.

We prescribed occupational lenses for 50–70 cm and asked her to move the screen to 65 cm. We also said those lenses were not for driving. At the six-week check she reported afternoons without headaches. The photographs carry two captions. Week 0 — 4 pm, second coffee: leaning toward the monitor, a slight squint. Week 6 — same desk, new lenses: thin metal glasses, sitting upright.

This is an individual account. Results differ. We cannot promise the same result. We can measure. A headache can have causes this clinic does not treat. The record here is the distance, the add, the lenses, the new screen position, and her report at six weeks.

the frame wall

the front row

L., 9, primary school

case two

L. is nine and in primary school. Parents and teacher described board blur and skipped lines. Reading material sat close to the face. The children's exam did not depend on fluent letter-chart reading. Picture targets and age-appropriate tasks carried the parts that needed them, with a parent in the room. Refraction showed mild myopia of −1.25 in both eyes.

The plan was a first pair of glasses, a front-row seat, and follow-up every six months. The front-row seat is a suggestion to the school so the board is usable. The six-month visits use the follow-up check: twenty minutes and $40 when the visit falls within six months of an exam here. Ines Kowalczyk fitted the first frames with the parent present. The children's exam itself is fifty minutes and $95.

The photographs show a boy trying frames at the pale wood wall with a parent, and later reading the board in new glasses. This is an individual account. Results differ. −1.25 is L.'s measurement, not a figure we expect from every child who skips a line.

week 0, the compress chair

week 8, evening, no burn

D., 31, software engineer

case three

D. is 31 and works as a software engineer. His eyes burned. His contact lenses felt uncomfortable by evening and acceptable earlier in the day. The dry eye evaluation looked at the surface and timed the tear film. Break-up was short. That matched the history: a heated office, a long screen day, a lens asked to last until night.

The plan had three parts. A lid care routine he could repeat at home, including a warm compress of the kind shown in the treatment-chair photograph. A change to daily lenses, so a drying lens was not asked to survive the whole day. And 20-20-20 breaks through the workday. The contact lens fitting is $110 and includes two follow-ups, which is how the lens change was reviewed. At eight weeks he was comfortable through the workday. The later photograph is that kind of evening: desk, laptop, a glass of water, eyes comfortable.

This is an individual account. Results differ. We are reporting D. at eight weeks. We are not publishing a timetable for the next engineer who books.

pages.title: Our Optometrists
pages.content:
Our Optometrists

seven people

Seven people work at Hitomi Vision. Dr. Elena Marsh and Samuel Achebe are pictured on this page. The other five are listed here by name, role, and the work they actually do.

Dr. Elena Marsh, OD

founder and director

Dr. Elena Marsh, OD

Founder and director.

Dr. Marsh sees adults, and she works on binocular vision: how the two eyes aim and hold a clear target at the distance the person actually uses. She opened Hitomi Vision in 2011 on the second floor of 14 Linden Row, Northgate, with three exam rooms and a small frame room. That is still the clinic.

Patients who want her for an adult binocular problem can ask for her by name. She is at the slit lamp herself, and the photograph on this page shows her there. The explanation at the end of a comprehensive exam is part of her standard. Fifteen minutes of the sixty-minute, $120 visit are reserved for the plan, so the findings are spoken in the room.

The other six people on this page cover children's vision, dry eye and contact lenses, screen and workplace vision, frames, imaging, and the book. Ask at the desk if you are unsure who should see you. Hana Lindgren would rather match the visit than fill a gap in the diary.

Samuel Achebe

imaging

Samuel Achebe

Clinical technician,
imaging.

Samuel Achebe runs the retinal camera and the other imaging the optometrist has asked for. You meet him when a visit includes that record. The screen beside him shows the image for the clinician to read; he does not replace the explanation stage. He is not an optometrist, he does not fit contact lenses, and he does not choose frames.

His work sits inside the ten-minute eye-health stage of a comprehensive exam, so the fifteen-minute explanation still has its full time. If imaging is not part of your plan, you may not meet him, and that is a clinical decision rather than an omission. The photograph on this page is him beside the camera, in the same bright exam room as the rest of the clinic.

Questions about what the image means belong with the optometrist who ordered it. Questions about the time of your visit belong with the front desk.

Also at the clinic

five more names

Dr. Tomas Reyes, OD

Children's vision and myopia follow-up

Dr. Reyes sees ages five to fifteen. The children's vision exam is fifty minutes and $95. Where a child cannot comfortably read a letter chart, he uses games and picture targets, and he takes the history from the parent in the room. Signs he expects to hear include a book held close, skipped lines, reading avoided, eyes rubbed, and a board that blurs from the back row.

Dr. Priya Nair, OD

Dry eye and contact lenses

The dry eye evaluation with Dr. Nair is forty minutes and $90: tear film, lids at the slit lamp, and a lid-care routine you can repeat at home when that is the finding. A warm compress in the treatment chair is part of teaching that routine, not a separate fee.

Dr. Jonah Whitfield, OD

Screen and workplace vision

The assessment is forty-five minutes and $85. Dr. Whitfield measures the distance to your screen, looks at monitor height, and decides whether occupational lenses, a separate desk pair, or distance glasses match the work. The 20-20-20 habit — every twenty minutes, a look about twenty feet away, for about twenty seconds — is discussed when a pause belongs in the plan. It is not offered in place of a lens.

Ines Kowalczyk

Optician, frames and lens fitting

Ines Kowalczyk fits frames and lenses after a prescription is known. She does not refract. Frames in the room start at $160. If the frame you prefer is above that starting price, she tells you before it is ordered. Lenses are quoted only once the exam, or a prescription you brought, says what they must do.

Hana Lindgren

Front desk and scheduling

Hana Lindgren answers +1 555 0142 208 and hello@hitomivision.example. She will ask which visit you need so the length is right: sixty minutes for a comprehensive exam at $120, fifty for a child at $95, forty-five for screen work at $85, forty for dry eye at $90, the contact lens fitting at $110 with its two follow-ups, or a twenty-minute follow-up at $40.

pages.content:
Visit and Book

second floor, linden row

Hitomi Vision is on the second floor of 14 Linden Row, Northgate. Take the lift from the street door. Hana Lindgren confirms every booking by phone or email.

Finding the second floor

how to find us

Look for the window
with the plants.

From the street, look for a front window with plants and a pale display of frames. The clinic does not use a large sign. The street door leads to a lift, and the rooms are on the second floor of 14 Linden Row, Northgate. You come out into the waiting room first. Three exam rooms and the frame room are along the same corridor. You do not pass through a shop to reach the chair.

The window photograph is that street view. The waiting-room photograph is the pale sofa, the side table, and the plant, empty and bright. Those two pictures are the whole of the approach. If you are early, you wait on the sofa. Hana Lindgren is at the desk.

If the row is unfamiliar, call +1 555 0142 208 and she will describe the window again. The email is hello@hitomivision.example. Give yourself time for the lift. The clinical hour starts when the history starts, and the history is worth starting on time.

These hours cover comprehensive exams, children's exams, screen assessments, dry eye visits, contact lens fittings, follow-up checks, and time in the frame room. A comprehensive exam is sixty minutes, so it needs a start that finishes by close. A twenty-minute follow-up is easier to place near the end of a day. Saturday closes at 16:00. Hana will only offer a time the visit can finish.

The same hours are published in every language, just as the fees are published in US dollars on every version of the site. If you write to us outside these hours, the message waits for the next open day. The clinic phone is answered when the desk is open.

Book an exam inside these hours. The chair is real time with one of the optometrists, not a walk-in queue.

Children's slots

after school

Children's after-school slots sit inside the opening hours. Monday to Friday, 15:30–18:30. Saturday, 9:00–12:00. They are for the children's vision exam, ages five to fifteen, fifty minutes, $95, with Dr. Tomas Reyes.

Say the child's age when you book. A parent stays for the visit. Games and picture targets are used when reading a chart is not realistic, so a young child does not need to rehearse letters beforehand. Bring current glasses if there are any, and a school note if a teacher has described the board or the reading.

First glasses, when they are needed, can be chosen with Ines Kowalczyk on the same afternoon if the frame room is free. If it is not, Hana books a fitting rather than rushing the wall. Frames start at $160. Myopia follow-up, when myopia is the finding, is every six months. The clinic is closed on Sunday and public holidays, including for these slots.

What to send when you book

ask for a time

Call +1 555 0142 208 or email hello@hitomivision.example. Leave your name, the kind of visit, and a phone number. For a child, add the age. If you wear contact lenses, say so. The contact form on this page asks for the same facts: name, email, phone, and a short note about the visit you want. It does not confirm the chair by itself. Hana confirms the time during opening hours.

Write which fee you are expecting so we can correct a mismatch before the day: $120 for sixty minutes, $95 for a child, $85 for screen work, $90 for dry eye, $110 for a contact lens fitting with two follow-ups, or $40 for a follow-up check within six months. Keep clinical detail for the history stage of the exam, where it can be recorded properly. A sentence on the form is enough to choose the right length.

We reply to the address you give. Please use an email you read.

On the day

the day itself

Arrive so the history can start at the time you were given. The comprehensive exam is sixty minutes of clinical work, from history through to the plan. The shorter visits are fifty, forty-five, forty, or twenty minutes, as published. Payment is the published fee for that visit, in US dollars. Receipts show the service, the date, the clinician, and the amount.

Frames ordered the same day are a separate charge, from $160, and lenses are quoted before you agree. You can also take the prescription and decide later. Nothing in the frame room is added without a figure spoken first.

If you are unwell and need to move the time, phone the desk so the room can be offered on. We would rather rebook you inside the week than hold an empty exam room. The address, again, is 2nd floor, 14 Linden Row, Northgate. Lift from the street door. Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00, Saturday 9:00–16:00.

pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
Privacy

what we keep

This page says what Hitomi Vision collects when you book or attend, who uses it, and how the public pages differ from a clinical record.

What you give us when you book

booking

When you book, we ask for your name, a phone number, an email address, and the kind of visit. The form on the visit page collects those fields and a short note. Phone calls to +1 555 0142 208 and emails to hello@hitomivision.example carry the same facts. We use them to confirm the appointment and to answer the question you sent.

At the exam we record the history, the measurements, and the plan. That is the clinical record of the visit you booked: the sixty-minute comprehensive exam, the children's exam, the screen assessment, the dry eye evaluation, the contact lens fitting, or the follow-up. Receipts show the service, the date, the clinician, and the amount in US dollars.

The three case stories on this site use an initial, an age, and a kind of work. They are individual accounts. They are not a list of patients, and they are not an invitation to send us clinical photographs through the form.

Who sees the record

the record

The optometrist who sees you uses the record to carry out the exam and any follow-up you have agreed, including a check within six months. Samuel Achebe, the clinical technician, sees the imaging he is asked to take. Ines Kowalczyk sees the prescription and the frame measurements when you order glasses. Hana Lindgren sees the booking details she needs to run the diary: name, contact, type of visit, and time.

We use contact details to confirm and to reply. We do not use them as a mailing list you did not ask for. A journal on the site is public writing about how we work. Searching the site does not create an account, and it does not open your clinical record.

You may ask the desk for your receipt or for a copy of your prescription details by phoning or emailing during opening hours. Monday to Friday 10:00–19:00, Saturday 9:00–16:00. The clinic is at 2nd floor, 14 Linden Row, Northgate.

Fees, messages, and the public site

messages and the site

Prices on the public pages are the prices in the room: $120, $95, $85, $90, $110, and $40, with frames from $160. Showing them here does not create an account. A form message or an email becomes correspondence about a booking. Keep medical history for the exam itself, where it is written into the clinical record rather than left in a short note.

The public case stories stay at the level already published. We do not add surnames, photographs of identified patients, or outcomes beyond the three accounts. Results in those accounts differ from person to person, and the pages say so.

If you wrote to us in error, say so in a reply and we will treat the message as withdrawn. For anything about a visit that is already in the book, the front desk is the right place: +1 555 0142 208 or hello@hitomivision.example.

categories.description: Working distance, breaks and tired eyes at the desk.

posts.title: The 20-20-20 habit, measured
posts.excerpt: The 20-20-20 habit is a timed look into the distance, and at Hitomi Vision it is added only after working distance, refraction, and the tear film have been measured.
posts.content:
The 20-20-20 habit is a break with three numbers built into its name. Every twenty minutes at a screen, you look at something about twenty feet away, and you keep looking for about twenty seconds. Then you go back to the work. Hitomi Vision teaches it inside a plan, not as a plan by itself. Dr. Jonah Whitfield may put it in a screen-work assessment. Dr. Priya Nair may put it beside lid care and a change of contact lens. Neither of them offers the timer in place of a measurement.

People arrive knowing the phrase. Some have tried it for a day. Some have a note under the keyboard. What is less common is a record of the distance to the screen, the lens in front of the eyes, and the time of day the symptoms start. A habit without those three is hard to judge. The screen-work eye assessment is forty-five minutes and $85, and it exists for that judgement. We write down how far the monitor sits, how high it is, when the eyes tire, and what the refraction wants at that range. When the question is wider than the desk, the comprehensive exam is sixty minutes and $120. Fifteen minutes at the end of that hour are the explanation. That is where a habit either earns a place or is left out.

M.'s account shows the order we prefer. She is 46 and works as an accountant. Headaches arrived at four o'clock. Her screen was at 55 centimetres. We measured a near add of +0.75 and prescribed occupational lenses for 50 to 70 centimetres. She moved the screen to 65 centimetres. At the six-week check she reported afternoons without headaches. The lenses and the distance were the changes we prescribed. Breaks may have helped her keep the new arrangement. We did not isolate them, and we will not pretend we did. This is an individual account. Results differ. We cannot promise the same afternoon to the next person in the chair. We can measure.

The twenty feet in the habit is a looking distance, not a prescription. The twenty minutes is an interval you either keep or forget. The twenty seconds is long enough for a focus to ease and for a few full blinks, which matters when the complaint is burning as well as blur. None of the three replaces the phoropter. If the chart is soft, looking across the room will not sharpen it. If the two eyes struggle to hold a near target together, that finding belongs in the binocular stage of the exam. Dr. Elena Marsh, who founded the clinic in 2011 and directs adult binocular work, would rather spend those ten minutes on the finding than send you home with only a timer. The habit sits downstream of the measurements, inside the plan.

Dryness is the other reason the pause comes up. Heated winter offices and a screen that reduces blinking are a hard combination for the tear film, the surface you actually look through. Vision can smear even when the refraction is sound. In the dry eye evaluation, forty minutes and $90, Dr. Nair looks at that surface and at the lids, and she times the break-up instead of asking you to guess. D. is 31 and works as a software engineer. His lenses were uncomfortable by evening, and his tear break-up was short. The plan was lid care, daily lenses, and 20-20-20 breaks. The contact lens fitting is $110 and includes two follow-ups, so the new lens was reviewed after real days of wear. At eight weeks he was comfortable through the workday. Again, one account. The breaks were one of three changes. Keeping a drying lens and adding only a timer is not a copy of his plan.

We are plain about the visits this habit does not replace. A child who holds a book close, skips lines, or cannot see the board needs the children's vision exam: fifty minutes, $95, ages five to fifteen, with Dr. Tomas Reyes. Games and picture targets are used when a letter chart is not fair. L., nine, had mild myopia of −1.25 in both eyes, a first pair of glasses, a front-row seat, and follow-up every six months. That is a refraction story. It is not a workplace break rule. Frames, when any of these plans includes glasses, start at $160. Ines Kowalczyk quotes the lenses after the exam, because an occupational range and a distance pair are different orders. A follow-up check within six months is twenty minutes and $40, and it is where we ask whether the afternoon changed.

If you try the habit before you come in, keep it simple. Use an interval you can remember. Look far, out of the screen, not at a second screen across the room. Notice the clock time when discomfort usually starts. M. named four o'clock. If you have a time of your own, bring it. Notice whether a pause shifts that time or leaves it where it was. Those observations belong in the history. Ten minutes at the start of a comprehensive exam are set aside for symptoms, and a specific afternoon is more useful than a general sense that screens are tiring.

The clinic is on the second floor of 14 Linden Row, Northgate, by the lift from the street door. Hours are Monday to Friday, 10:00 to 19:00, and Saturday, 9:00 to 16:00. Sunday and public holidays are closed. Phone +1 555 0142 208, or email hello@hitomivision.example. Ask for a screen-work assessment if the desk is the question, or a dry eye evaluation if the burn arrives ahead of the blur. Name the visit you want, so the length in the book matches the problem. We will measure first. The habit can wait until we know what it is being asked to support.
